sections.topic_sentence: **Authority.** Who is entitled to exercise engineering judgment: to decide what a system must do, permit or refuse an action, and answer for the result.
**Agent.** An AI system that pursues an open-ended or underspecified task through multiple steps, exercising judgment about what to do next and using tools in response to intermediate results.
**Agentic engineering.** The engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work.

sections.heading_text: How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?
sections.topic_sentence: This is a book about engineering: what engineering becomes when reasoning capacity becomes abundant.
*Agentic engineering* is the engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work.

One way to understand MAGE is as a classical software-engineering move: **add a level of indirection.**[^indirection] Conventional engineering has long separated the engineering of an artifact from its physical realization.
MAGE grew out of an engineering problem I encountered while building DocAble, a service for making documents accessible to people with disabilities.
This book is for software engineers who want to understand what changes when implementation can be delegated to capable agents.

preamble_points.text: Coding agents make software implementation cheap enough to change the engineering problem, creating the question of what engineers should do with the new productive capacity.
A printer can produce many kinds of artifacts, subject to the capabilities and limitations of its machinery.
People make broad productive capacity useful by developing forms and ways of working.
Software agents supply broad productive capacity and can infer implementation decisions that incomplete instructions leave unspecified.
Delegation can leave useful judgment to the agent, but the engineer decides which decisions to make explicit and which to delegate.

sections.heading_text: Consequential Choices and Degrees of Freedom
sections.topic_sentence: Delegating implementation is useful only if we can avoid doing much of the implementation work ourselves.

points.text: Even a simple software specification leaves enormous freedom — ten lines or ten thousand, a monolith or microservices — so engineers can specify the properties that matter and leave other decisions to the intelligence performing the work; which choices can safely remain open is itself an engineering decision.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineers increasingly exercise those decisions through the environment in which agents work.

points.text: As implementation becomes abundant, engineering leverage moves toward the instructions, representations, constraints, evidence, and infrastructure that shape autonomous work.
A governed engineering environment carries engineering decisions forward by making consequential knowledge available, enforcing selected obligations, and preserving evidence for control.

sections.heading_text: When Agents Produce the Wrong Result
sections.topic_sentence: “’Tis a poor craftsman who blames his tools.” For an engineer, the aphorism directs attention to the work that precedes fabrication: representing the problem, choosing which properties must hold, and arranging how the result will be checked.

points.text: Before blaming productive machinery, examine the engineer’s work in representing the problem, choosing required properties, and arranging how the result will be checked.

Agent inference can fill gaps in the engineering supplied to it, hiding omissions; a completed artifact does not establish that the inferred choices satisfy the intended properties or acceptable tradeoffs.
Inspect the instructions, problem representation, task boundary, tools, and required evidence before diagnosing a capability limit; failed output alone does not establish that limit.
Abundant implementation raises the stakes: capable agents execute a bad direction at extraordinary speed, and velocity amplifies sound engineering and bad engineering alike.

sections.topic_sentence: In 2024, the U.S.

points.text: University document accessibility combines an explicit legal obligation, semantic and structural requirements, and institutional scale.
DocAble's requirements include genuine accessibility, preservation, accountability, and practical operation at scale.
Accessibility, preservation, accountability, and economical operation must be satisfied together.

sections.topic_sentence: While I was developing DocAble, the DOJ extended its original April 2026 compliance deadline for larger public entities by one year, to April 2027.

points.text: One project answered both problems: build the accessibility system, and use the engineering work to discover what sustained agentic development demanded.

sections.topic_sentence: From the user’s perspective, DocAble is simple: upload an inaccessible document; receive a remediated document and a changelog.

points.text: The user supplies an inaccessible document and receives a remediated document and a changelog.
Art, language instruction, and handwritten mathematics illustrate why accessible output depends on the document's educational purpose.
Semantic interpretation helps propose changes; reliable document processing and suitable evidence are needed to establish whether the result satisfies the obligations.

preamble_points.text: MAGE emerged from developing and studying DocAble; the case introduces the engineering experience behind the methodology.

sections.topic_sentence: As a professor of computer engineering, part of my job is to evaluate emerging technologies and decide what they mean for engineering practice and education.
The coding agents available in 2026 are built primarily around large language models, which serve as their **foundation models**.

points.text: Coding agents combine capabilities acquired through foundation-model training with harness facilities that turn responses into action; engineers can shape their operating environment without changing trained weights.

sections.topic_sentence: Predictive training can produce useful problem-solving capabilities and representations of the processes underlying a sequence.
Four properties of contemporary foundation models matter to the engineering argument.

points.text: Four properties of contemporary foundation models matter to engineering: broad semantic reasoning supports delegated implementation, probabilistic output calls for independent assurance, bounded working state motivates external representations, and inexpensive repeated reasoning increases the need for scalable governance.
Natural-language requests can leave consequential choices implicit, and iterative changes can lose earlier obligations; FlowCheck provides a concrete scheduler example.

sections.topic_sentence: An **agentic harness** is the runtime that turns the foundation model’s reasoning into action.

points.text: The harness supplies action through tools, context management, and interposition; it may also support task management and parallel execution.

Harness-engineering work treats autonomous capability as a property of the foundation-model–harness–environment system; MAGE focuses on the environment as a practical means of control and a place to preserve engineering knowledge beyond one reasoning episode.

sections.topic_sentence: Scale has always created problems.

points.text: Human working memory is limited even when long-term knowledge is extensive; notes, diagrams, and other external representations let engineers work with more information than they can hold actively in mind.
A harness can preserve and retrieve information across invocations, extending work beyond the model's immediate context; retaining a record does not ensure that the agent will find and use it.

Available information is not always used effectively: usable context can fall short of nominal capacity, information within a window is not uniformly accessible, and repository work incurs navigation and reconstruction costs.

The reasoning horizon is the practical limit of work the reasoner and its supporting machinery can carry through reliably, given the available representations and resources; task demands are distinct from this system-level limit.

The reasoning horizon grounds the Representation Problem: explicit representations can reduce task-state and reconstruction demands, and Modeling addresses how to preserve the properties relevant to an engineering question.

sections.topic_sentence: The second problem concerns assurance.

points.text: Software engineering has always separated authorship from assurance — we compile instead of trusting a prediction, test instead of accepting an explanation — because the producer's confidence is not enough.

Commodity intelligence makes that separation more important because implementation is cheap and repeatable; an agent can propose, inspect, explain, and repair, but another judgment from the same substrate does not constitute independent evidence — the environment must establish what evidence counts.
Decisions that depend on agentic inference form the probabilistic surface; mechanisms can enforce particular requirements even when the agent makes a mistake.

The Enforcement Problem asks how important obligations can bind autonomous work without relying on the agent remembering or self-certifying each time; Alignment addresses this problem alongside the Representation Problem already named at the reasoning horizon.

preamble_points.text: The DocAble experiment sought informed control over agent-produced implementation with almost no personal code inspection; this motivates examining the machinery's capabilities and limitations.

Engineering methods must fit the machinery they govern; observable capabilities, training, and the facilities around a foundation model help explain what engineers can delegate and how they can govern it.

Engineers can retain informed control through the system knowledge, instructions, tools, evidence, and mechanisms surrounding agentic work, without inspecting every implementation line or controlling internal learned representations.

Modeling makes consequential properties explicit and can reduce reconstruction or support assurance; Alignment connects selected obligations to constraints, evidence-producing sensors, and admission-controlling gates. They remain independent and can be combined selectively, as the DocAble content-preservation example demonstrates.

The engineering questions extend beyond software, while useful representations, credible evidence, and the appropriate balance of delegation and governance depend on the domain. The following chapters develop the mechanisms, practice, evidence, theory, and wider implications.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Is a Classical Engineering Move
sections.topic_sentence: Modeling is not new.

points.text: Modeling is not new: engineering has long used representations that suppress irrelevant detail so a property can be reasoned about directly.

These representations share one engineering move — choose a form in which the property of interest becomes easier to express, inspect, or analyze than in the implementation; MAGE proposes no new modeling language, and this chapter illustrates the technique through selected established models.
Established models preserve selected design knowledge outside implementation so agents can reuse it; each representation must justify its upkeep.

A useful model may be three states and two transitions, a list of permitted edges, or a schema joined on identifiers; the relevant question is what representation makes a recurring engineering question easier to answer.

sections.heading_text: A Model Is a Purposeful Reduction
sections.topic_sentence: A **model** is a purposeful reduction of a system.

points.text: A model is a purposeful reduction; its value is what it leaves out. The engineering question decides what to keep.
A model can record accurate facts yet omit a distinction needed for a decision: remaining prepaid credits cannot distinguish an exhausted allowance from unlimited service entitlement.
Obligations rarely fix one implementation; a tolerance bounds permitted variation, a degree of freedom is a choice left open.

sections.topic_sentence: Leaving detail out of a model can also be understood as preserving useful choices during implementation.

points.text: Preserving a degree of freedom defers a decision to a reasoner better positioned to make it: information may arrive later, and the implementing agent can acquire evidence before deciding.

Parsimony reasons from the proposed model inward: each distinction it contains must be required by the engineering question or removed; the aim is not the smallest model but the smallest model adequate to its purpose.
Reduction fails in either direction: too little reproduces complexity and may needlessly constrain implementation, while too much erases a consequential distinction.
MAGE favors models adequate to their purpose; both additional detail and greater semantic precision must justify their construction and maintenance costs.
Whether a distinction is needed remains an engineering judgment that can change with evidence; an omitted distinction may prove consequential, or a represented one unnecessary.
In software a tolerance can be numeric but is often qualitative, because code owes more to discrete mathematics than to continuous media.
A quantitative model can distinguish a target from a required limit, allowing engineers to reason about the remaining margin as well as whether the requirement is satisfied.

Obligations bound the space of acceptable implementations without selecting a point; commodity intelligence makes exercising that freedom cheap, so Modeling names the consequential distinctions and Alignment enforces selected boundaries.

The engineering problem sets the obligations regardless of the implementer; a more capable human or agent may need less scaffolding but still needs the relevant information in the model or from other evidence.
A tacit obligation can look free; the "not that" test reveals a boundary that was never written down.

sections.heading_text: Not every unmodeled choice is free
sections.topic_sentence: This also distinguishes tacit obligations from genuinely free choices.

points.text: Whether a choice is tacitly bounded or genuinely free is a present state, not a fixed one; it changes as engineers learn from the system.
Modeling can begin before specification is complete; a reduction can make variation tractable so distinctions can be discovered.
Hold the system constant, change the question, and the model changes; there is no single model of the system.
A model earns its place by the question it settles, not by how much of the system it represents.

Models may be encoded in types or held in an engineer’s understanding of code; modeling makes the relevant reduction available to other reasoners, and a different question may require another reduction.

A model adopted as a statement of requirements records which properties later implementations must preserve; purposeful reduction makes those decisions available for human review and agent use without reproducing every code detail.

sections.topic_sentence: These representations may be written as diagrams, tables, type declarations, or executable rules.

points.text: Purposeful reduction is a judgment process, not an algorithm: no procedure takes an engineering question and returns the right model, so the engineer reasons toward the boundary from more than one direction and revises it as evidence arrives.

Reasoning top-down from the question asks what must remain true and which distinctions expressing or evaluating that obligation requires; the model preserves those, and the remaining implementation choices stay free.

Reasoning bottom-up from the proposed model asks, for each represented distinction, what engineering question or obligation requires it; a distinction no consequential purpose justifies carrying is removed.

Neither direction guarantees the boundary is right; analysis, implementation, measurement, or failure may reveal that an omitted distinction mattered or an included one did not, and the model is revised when the evidence changes the engineering judgment.
Implementing and trying a design can reveal distinctions that were not evident in the initial model.

sections.topic_sentence: We can also learn what to model by building and trying an implementation.

points.text: An exploratory implementation can expose constraints, tradeoffs, state distinctions, dependencies, and bounds that were not evident in the initial design.
A prototype retains an implementation but may not explain what engineers learned from it; record the useful relationships explicitly so later work can use the lesson without repeating the experiment.

sections.topic_sentence: An exploratory implementation can introduce useful design choices that the engineer did not specify in advance.

points.text: An agent can introduce useful design choices through exploratory implementation, but the engineer must judge whether they suit the present system.
The agent may supply a design insight; the engineer takes responsibility for adopting it by evaluating it against the system's requirements.
Engineers record accepted design choices so later implementations can preserve the relevant relationships without reproducing incidental details.

Models can preserve both accepted obligations and descriptive observations; the representation should distinguish what later implementations must preserve from what engineers learned about the current one.
Tests can explicitly preserve accepted engineering decisions; engineers choose what the tests should require, make their purpose clear, and decide how the environment should act on failures.

sections.heading_text: Structure and Semantics Make Representations Machine-Operable
sections.topic_sentence: A model can preserve the right distinctions without completely defining what those distinctions mean.

points.text: A representation can preserve the right distinctions while its interpreters supply most of its meaning.
Semantic commitment: how much meaning the representation itself carries explicitly.
Purposeful reduction determines which distinctions to preserve; semantic commitment determines how precisely the representation defines them.
Stronger semantics buy capabilities and create obligations; they are not inherently better.
Concrete artifacts illustrate the range; the rows are examples, not maturity levels.
Stronger commitment aids mechanical interpretation; it moves interpretation burden rather than removing it.
Semantic precision and generative completeness are different properties.

sections.topic_sentence: Consider three boxes labeled Reporting, BillingAPI, and BillingDB, representing a reporting service, the billing API, and the billing database.

points.text: Giving Calls a declared direct-invocation interpretation separates syntax from meaning; the model's purpose and scope determine whether recorded and omitted pairs describe observations or specify permitted behavior.
A partial transition function defines the intended effects of start, finish, and fail over the same four-state job lifecycle used later; undefined pairs admit no lifecycle transition.
Structure — an explicit declared shape a machine can read — is what lets a representation be traversed, checked, and joined.
The simplest useful form of externalized knowledge is a graph of engineering entities and their relations; graph names the structure, not the storage.
Shape does not distinguish representations, semantics do; semantic commitment decides how much of that meaning is declared rather than understood.
Externalizing knowledge is the lightest form of Modeling; catalogs, named obligations, reusable skills, and connected registries preserve knowledge for later work.
Explicit semantics preserve meanings that later agents would otherwise have to infer without the shared context of the original team.

sections.topic_sentence: A model’s structure and semantics determine what tools can do with it.

points.text: Increasing semantic commitment can make additional capabilities possible — not a required sequence or maturity model.

sections.topic_sentence: Software engineers do not need to invent a representation from first principles each time they encounter a consequential question.

points.text: Software engineers need not invent a representation from first principles each time; engineering fields have accumulated a large repertoire of models for recurring questions, each preserving different information and supporting different analyses.
What matters is not a representation's graphical shape but the engineering question its entities and relations preserve.
The practical skill is recognizing the engineering question and selecting a representation that preserves the properties needed to answer it; MAGE prescribes no new notation.

This chapter illustrates modeling practice rather than exhausting it; once the engineering question is known, start with the representations the field has already developed — the repertoire is reusable engineering knowledge, and choosing from it remains engineering judgment.

preamble_points.text: A foundation model knows the languages and patterns; it does not know your system — those facts live in the engineered environment.
The first modeling move is simple: externalize engineering knowledge that should not have to be rediscovered.

Natural language is a representation, and often an appropriate one; consequential knowledge kept only in prose must be articulated correctly and then recovered correctly by each later reasoner, and a structured model can preserve distinctions that would otherwise be restated or reconstructed.
Models help engineers make decisions and detect omissions as well as helping agents interpret engineering knowledge.
The Modeling Principle in its weakest form: externalize engineering knowledge into explicit, structured models to reason through.

sections.heading_text: The Canonical Move: Structure and Dependency
sections.topic_sentence: A component diagram names which services exist; a dependency graph names which modules rest on which; a call graph names which procedures may invoke which; a data-flow diagram names how information moves through transformations; a deployment topology names what is connected across execution locations.

points.text: Component and dependency graphs, call graphs, data-flow diagrams, and deployment topologies all name the entities a question needs and the declared relations between them, and drop the behavior.

A structural model selects the entities a question needs and the relations between them; the edge label specifies the relationship being modeled, so a generic "related-to" edge discards the distinction the model exists to preserve.

Explicit structure turns the claims an engineer wants into graph properties — local, path, or whole-graph — and the analyses into ordinary graph operations: reachability, reverse traversal, cycle detection, impact and conformance.

Static analysis can derive the graph from code and engineers can declare it as intent; one describes what the system appears to do, the other what it is supposed to do, and Chapter 3 treats the difference.

sections.heading_text: Choose the Relation for the Question
sections.topic_sentence: Suppose a web application's user interface should reach its database only through an application service.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Behavior with States and Transitions
sections.topic_sentence: For lifecycle and recovery questions, a state-transition model makes explicit which states matter and how the system can move between them.

points.text: State-transition models make lifecycle and recovery questions explicit; state machines, labeled transition systems, and statecharts represent behavior, while temporal specifications state properties over executions.
Reducing a service to states and transitions turns "can it reach a state it should never occupy?" from a reconstruction over scattered handlers into a question a person or tool can answer.

A behavioral model represents states and transitions; it can specify allowed behavior or describe behavior to be checked against a requirement. Safety and liveness properties ask different questions over the admitted executions.

sections.topic_sentence: When several workers can process the same job, *who owns this job?* depends on their claims.

points.text: Concurrent workers can acquire, lose, and regain rights to a job; locks, leases, capabilities, and claims express different aspects of access and ownership, which the model selects according to the question.

A claim binds a holder to a resource and carries which holder, which generation of claim, and when it expires — the generation being what tells a current claim from a superseded one — and because the hard failures live in interleavings, the characteristic analysis is state-space exploration with invariant checking.

The model omits the processing topology: ownership, generation, lifetime, and reclamation are the consequential properties, and the implementation later changed how the job's work is partitioned without invalidating the model — the pointers to the code changed, not the model.

sections.topic_sentence: A lease illustrates how one representation can answer several classes of question.

points.text: Read as ownership the lease says who controls a job; read as behavioral it traces a claimed-held-expired-reclaimed lifecycle; counted, it measures how much work is in flight — one representation, three questions.

The overlap follows from the distinction introduced at the chapter's opening: model classes identify engineering questions, not mutually exclusive data structures — the observation the closing section builds on to connect the models.

sections.heading_text: The Canonical Move: Choosing Among Alternatives
sections.topic_sentence: Decision tables map conditions to choices; rule systems state how evidence affects a decision; constraint systems distinguish admissible alternatives.

points.text: Decision tables, rule systems, and constraint systems make choices explicit; policy is one kind of decision model, expressed through access-control matrices, policy graphs, and feature models as well as those general forms.

An observed-call edge and a permitted-call edge can look identical while answering different questions; in the illustrated models, a missing edge means no recorded call or no permitted call respectively.

Once permission is declared, the claims a policy designer wants become expressible — permitted/forbidden, mutual exclusion, prerequisites, consistency, completeness, least privilege — and "is this allowed?" becomes an evaluation rather than an argument.

sections.heading_text: Compare the Decision with the Facts
sections.topic_sentence: In a hypothetical system, a public web interface may call a report service, which may in turn call a renderer.

sections.heading_text: Preserve the Cases a Decision Must Distinguish
sections.topic_sentence: The input representation can make a decision wrong before any rule is evaluated.

sections.heading_text: When the Decision Depends on Context
sections.topic_sentence: Some decisions cannot be made from the object alone.

points.text: An image's informational role depends on context; DocAble uses a VLM classification with an explicit conservative policy that retains content when the classification is uncertain.

sections.topic_sentence: A **modeling substrate** is the collection of representations through which engineers and agents can recover and relate system knowledge.

points.text: Shared identities let different representations refer to the same service, work item, or operation without requiring a common file format or metamodel.
Prefer shared identity and derivation over independently maintained copies of the same fact; where duplication is unavoidable, make the correspondence explicit and checkable.

sections.topic_sentence: A static model and a history answer different questions.

points.text: A static model and a history answer different questions; stable task identity permits a join when observations help answer a structural question.
A provenance model selects the history needed to answer an engineering question rather than recording every observable event.

sections.topic_sentence: Some answers require a join.

points.text: Joining models makes properties that cross individual representations available for reasoning.
A join can preserve entity identity while losing a distinction needed by the decision; shared identity does not establish semantic adequacy.
An engineer or agent can begin at the entity named by a task and follow the modeled relationships required by its engineering question.

sections.topic_sentence: Models and implementations can fall out of correspondence as a system changes.

points.text: Multiple models can diverge from the system or one another; the correspondence mechanism depends on which representation owns each fact.

Maintain correspondence according to the source of truth: derive a view from implementation, generate an artifact from a model or read the model during execution, or maintain traceability where neither side fully determines the other.

sections.heading_text: Derive when implementation owns the truth
sections.topic_sentence: The model is a projection of the implementation.

sections.heading_text: When the model is the source of truth
sections.topic_sentence: **Generation** produces an artifact from a model: code, configuration, or documentation.

points.text: A runner can read a task model to determine dependency order and readiness without generating a separate artifact.
A derived analytical graph still omits implementation detail, and derivation preserves only its declared correspondence rather than establishing architecture quality.

Where neither model nor implementation fully determines the other, traceability records a defined relationship between model elements and current implementation targets so engineers and agents can inspect correspondence and assess the impact of changes.

sections.heading_text: Trace and check where neither owns the truth
sections.topic_sentence: Where neither side can be fully derived from the other, **traceability** records their relationship explicitly.

points.text: Model coverage has a revisable boundary: some claims are mechanically decidable, others require semantic judgment, and unmodeled properties have no model-based coverage; experience may justify representing a new property or removing an unnecessary distinction.

sections.topic_sentence: The boundary of what engineers choose to model can change with experience.

points.text: A structured schema plus checked predicates is one executable-model pattern; generation, simulation, transformation, and analysis are others, and correspondence to a changing system still requires checks or derivations.
Synchronization does not establish that the model is correct; a model can be perfectly in sync and still express the wrong architecture.

Correspondence follows the source of truth: derive an implementation view, generate an artifact or interpret an authoritative model, and trace and check where neither representation fully determines the other.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Makes Properties Available to Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: Modeling makes a property explicit; engineers decide how to use it.

points.text: A worker-pool model makes quantities and capacity comparisons explicit; engineers still choose whether to use them for planning, admission tuning, or a hard refusal.
A measurement model defines quantities and their reference bounds; observation, adaptation, and enforcement require separate decisions and mechanisms, and model analysis also guides design.

preamble_points.text: Different questions require different models of one system; shared identity and explicit correspondence connect them where a question crosses views.

sections.heading_text: Reasoning Input, Action, Work Unit, and Artifact/Runtime
sections.topic_sentence: The first location is **reasoning input**: the context, representations, examples, and instructions put in front of the reasoner.

points.text: The first location is reasoning input: ordinarily guidance, not enforcement.
The first enforcement boundary is the action: one attempted side effect the harness can inspect or refuse.
The second enforcement boundary is the work unit, where whole-work obligations become legible.
The third enforcement boundary is the artifact or runtime: forbidden state made impossible to express or accept.

sections.heading_text: Placement and Strength Are Different Decisions
sections.topic_sentence: These locations do not form a monotonic scale from weak to strong.

points.text: The four boundaries do not form a monotonic weak-to-strong scale.
Substantial enforcement can exist without rich models; richer models expand the properties the environment can state and govern.

sections.heading_text: Return Evidence at the Earliest Useful Boundary
sections.topic_sentence: The boundaries also determine what feedback can return and when.

points.text: Boundary placement affects what feedback can return and when; timely evidence lets an agent use the reasoning and context already at hand, while delayed feedback may require reconstruction.
These mechanisms do not act independently; the interplay is its own problem, deferred to §3.5.

The Alignment Principle, stated whole: make engineering obligations enforceable by encoding them into mechanisms — constrain, sense, evaluate, admit — that can enforce them; in other words, once an obligation is entrusted to the engineering environment, satisfying it should not depend solely on each future agent remembering it.

preamble_points.text: The environment intervenes between a proposed action and its consequence.
Guidance influences behavior; enforcement determines what the environment permits or accepts, and feedback returns evidence between them.
Recent agentic-security guidance draws a similar boundary: secure the process that produces the artifact.
An obligation can be enforced at several boundaries; choose where it is visible and a mechanism can enforce it.

sections.topic_sentence: A drift check can establish a declared correspondence between two artifacts.

points.text: A drift check establishes agreement between two artifacts, not that the correspondence expresses the right intent.
The distinction is not derived versus authored; it is description versus independent obligation.
Drift checking has a precise job: preserve a declared correspondence between model and implementation; correctness needs another claim.
Proofs and model checks evaluate stated properties under their assumptions; they do not establish that the chosen properties capture the engineering requirement.
Fix the required behavior before choosing an analysis; independence concerns the source of the obligation and the implementation judged against it.
Three different relations matter — correspondence, conformance, or acceptance — and they are not interchangeable.

sections.topic_sentence: A second problem is placement.

points.text: An obligation can be stated clearly and still be unenforceable at the boundary where you try to check it.
Checking model drift at the commit is the wrong granularity; the property belongs to the completed unit of work.
Test the served page in a browser at the earliest boundary where the relevant composition can be exercised; a successful HTTP fetch alone does not establish correct rendering.

sections.topic_sentence: Both examples illustrate the same rule for placing enforcement:

points.text: The design rule: place enforcement at the earliest boundary where the obligation is both legible and decidable.
The rhyme: Modeling chooses the reduction that answers the question without carrying unnecessary detail; Alignment chooses the earliest boundary where the obligation is legible.
Real boundaries are sometimes approximate: a hook that fires early enough to leave budget for the work beats the theoretically ideal hook.
The section has supplied both requirements for enforcement; the next question is what the mechanism at that boundary actually does.

preamble_points.text: Enforcement needs an obligation independent of the work being judged, and a boundary at which that obligation is legible.
An obligation may live in a model, or directly in a type, permission, schema, test, or policy; Alignment does not require a particular representation.
Requirements traceability connects intent, implementation, and evidence to support evaluation and change analysis.

Traceability can relate an obligation, its realization, and its evidence without any mechanism enforcing the obligation — a requirement can trace cleanly to a test whose failure is merely reported, and a permission boundary can enforce firmly without a rich traceability model.
Where an obligation permits variation, the acceptable region must come from governing intent, not from the realization being judged.
Two lessons: agreement is not correctness, and placement must follow the meaning of the obligation.

sections.topic_sentence: A constraint can exclude some violations before they occur.

points.text: Constraints exclude particular actions or states; sensors supply evidence about behavior that remains possible.
The accompanying note connects constraints and feedback to systems-safety engineering without identifying agent engineering with a control system.
An instruction is enforced only when a mechanism in the environment acts on it.
A constraint excludes particular actions or representations within the scope of its language, interface, or runtime permissions; a closed type does not govern every possible behavior.
A generator can embody selected obligations in implementation structure; this requires a valid model, a property-preserving transformation, and protection against bypass.
Agents can construct checkers or controls for explicit obligations; generating a checker does not establish the checked implementation's correctness.
A sensor produces evidence about artifacts, attempted actions, or observed executions; observability exposes the state or behavior that the environment must inspect.
Evidence must preserve the distinctions needed to judge the obligation, such as caller identity, destination, and architectural component.

sections.topic_sentence: A gate evaluates a condition and permits or refuses passage, drawing on evidence it checks directly or receives from another checker.

points.text: A gate evaluates whether an action or result may proceed, locally or through a delegated check, and enforces the decision; a blocking check can reject both genuine violations and false positives.
Instrumented tests produce observations, a checker compares them with the architectural model, and the merge gate requires the build and interaction checks to pass.
The merge gate uses build and interaction check results to decide whether a candidate meets its admission conditions.
Defense in depth combines protections with different coverage; tests and the gate that enforces their results constitute one protection together.
Human review can combine tacit context, evaluation, and approval; selected obligations in agentic work need explicit rules, evidence, and admission consequences.
A release check can regenerate evidence from the actual candidate and evaluate it independently of the producing agent; reuse requires unchanged relevant inputs.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble’s PDF changeset interface provides an action boundary for document repair.

points.text: In DocAble's PDF changeset interface, a closed operation vocabulary constrains proposals, the applier refuses unsupported targets or missing evidence, and subsequent validation checks selected properties of the resulting document.

sections.topic_sentence: The reporting-service boundary concerns relationships among components.

sections.heading_text: One Obligation, Several Ways to Hold It
sections.topic_sentence: A modeled obligation does not imply one particular enforcement technology.

points.text: Generation, runtime constraints, tests, and model checking supply different kinds of restriction or evidence and can be combined for the obligation at hand.
An atomic conditional update can prevent competing claimants from both acquiring the same claim; tests and analysis can examine the surrounding protocol.
Model checking explores the behavior admitted by an explicit model; model-based testing exercises an implementation against expected model behavior.
A universal eventuality claim requires reasoning about modeled executions and stated scheduling or recovery assumptions; a finite passing test does not establish it.
In DocAble, a lease makes abandoned work recoverable, while a separate durable claim restricts who may perform the protected effect; recovery alone does not supply that permission.
Select and combine mechanisms according to the evidence or restriction they contribute and the cost of obtaining it.
A check may remain advisory; a gate must act on the result when it is intended to control whether work may proceed.

sections.topic_sentence: The reporting service’s usage measurements can support several responses, depending on the policy attached to them.

points.text: One quantitative model can support observation, adaptation, graceful degradation, or hard admission control; the appropriate response depends on the obligation attached to the quantity.
A quantitative tolerance can expose margin — the room between the realized value and its bound; two conforming realizations can differ in how much room they keep.
Margin is computable only where the model supplies a meaningful distance; many software obligations are qualitative and admit none.

sections.topic_sentence: The reporting-service rule forbids a particular access.

points.text: A constraint can forbid an action or require an evidence-producing one; provenance shows the positive form.

sections.topic_sentence: The reporting-service example concerns which components may interact.

points.text: Provenance is useful for a particular architectural-conformance problem: the required relation is the path through which a protected operation was derived, not merely which components interact.

sections.heading_text: What Does a Software Factory Produce?
sections.topic_sentence: The analogy requires one adjustment before we apply it to software.

points.text: The analogy needs one adjustment: a physical factory commonly produces many instances of a product, while a software service may be one continuously evolving system and another copy of a program costs almost nothing.

The output of a software factory is not another copy of the product but the next working realization of it: each production cycle begins with a working software system and attempts to produce a changed system that still works.
A software factory organizes controlled change while preserving control over consequential properties and consequences.
A software factory includes a GEE of reusable representations, tools, procedures, and controls, together with its people, agents, production activities, and organizational authority.

The difference respecializes the two problems of factory engineering: process design organizes the production of changes, and tolerance constrains how much freedom the fabricator may exercise while the changed product remains acceptable, so the factory produces new realizations of an evolving artifact rather than copies of the same one.

Realizing controlled change carries a cost physical manufacturing can amortize differently: a drawing stays useful across thousands of instances of a part, while a representation of a software system describes a target that is itself being changed, so engineering artifacts incur a carrying cost.

Software organizations have made different economic judgments about that cost — some find durable value in explicit representations, others find it cheaper to keep skilled engineers close to implementation — and the tradeoff turns on how much reusable knowledge a representation carries and how expensive it is to keep accurate.

The Agile movement placed substantially greater weight on keeping knowledgeable humans close to implementation, which makes particular sense when the object of engineering is controlled change: a representation that does not change with the software can cease to describe the thing it is meant to govern.

Earlier attempts to separate engineering judgment from implementation met the same tradeoff from the other direction: moving decisions upstream let less experienced programmers implement, but only if costly representations carried the judgment they would otherwise supply.

The economic question was never whether software should use models but where engineering judgment could be carried most economically without losing control: craft production stays economical when transferring judgment out of fabrication costs as much as leaving it there, and factory production becomes economical when reusable structures carry it more cheaply.
Inexpensive capable agents can resolve ordinary implementation choices while the production system preserves selected consequential judgments and acceptance evidence.

sections.heading_text: The Two Rules of Agentic Software Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: I began with two rules.

points.text: Not reading the code was deliberate: inspecting agent-produced implementation would have bounded implementation throughput by the engineer's own reading capacity, so the first rule made reading the last resort and an engineering environment the surface through which work was directed and judged.

The rule did not forbid reading source: needing to read it pointed to a missing supervisory surface — a model, test, lint, instrument, or architectural boundary — so reading was the escape hatch, not the operating model.

The second rule required the resulting system to be good, fast, and cheap — partly a DocAble requirement, partly a test of whether agents could help build a production system good enough to trust, fast enough to matter, and cheap enough to deploy at scale.

A fast factory producing poor software would fail the test, and so would a high-quality system that stayed prohibitively expensive to develop or operate; agentic implementation was valuable only if the engineering system around it achieved all three.
